claim: HRMAn is an open-source image analysis platform based on machine learning algorithms and deep learning.
source: We present HRMAn (Host Response to Microbe Analysis), an open-source image analysis platform based on machine learning algorithms and deep learning.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract describing the nature of the software platform.

claim: HRMAn has the capacity to learn phenotypes from the data, without relying on researcher-based assumptions.
source: We show that HRMAn has the capacity to learn phenotypes from the data, without relying on researcher-based assumptions.
evidence: Stated as a demonstrated capability in the abstract.

claim: HRMAn can recognize, classify and quantify pathogen killing, replication and cellular defense responses using Toxoplasma gondii and Salmonella enterica Typhimurium.
source: Using Toxoplasma gondii and Salmonella enterica Typhimurium we demonstrate HRMAn's capacity to recognize, classify and quantify pathogen killing, replication and cellular defense responses.
evidence: Demonstrated capability stated in the abstract with specific pathogens tested.

claim: HRMAn is suitable for both single image and high content image analysis.
source: HRMAn thus presents the only intelligent solution operating at human capacity suitable for both single image and high content image analysis.
evidence: Stated capability in the abstract.

claim: High content imaging has revolutionized the field of host–pathogen interaction by allowing large-scale compound and host genome-wide depletion screens.
source: High content imaging (HCI) has revolutionized the field of host–pathogen interaction by allowing researchers to perform image-based large-scale compound and host genome-wide depletion screens in a high-throughput fashion (Brodin and Christophe, 2011; Mattiazzi Usaj et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The majority of host-pathogen interaction screens assess interactions using bulk colorimetric or automated enumeration of pathogen growth at the population level.
source: The majority of these screens assess host–pathogen interactions using bulk colorimetric or automated enumeration of pathogen growth at the population level (Ang and Pethe, 2016; Radke et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Quantification of host–pathogen interaction is often performed manually.
source: Additionally, quantification of host–pathogen interaction (e.g. analysis of host protein recruitment to the pathogen) in general is often performed manually.
evidence: Statement about current practice in the field.

claim: To meaningfully dissect cell-mediated pathogen control, it is imperative to quantify the host response and pathogen fate at the single-cell level.
source: However, to meaningfully dissect cell-mediated pathogen control, it is imperative to quantify the host response and pathogen fate at the single-cell level.
evidence: Statement of scientific necessity based on biological reasoning.

claim: Many open-source and proprietary analysis software packages have been developed for host-pathogen interaction analysis.
source: Many open-source, e.g. CellProfiler (Carpenter et al., 2006), and proprietary, e.g. Perkin Elmer Harmony, analysis software packages have been developed and successfully employed for this purpose (Eliceiri et al., 2012; Stöter et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to existing software and publications.

claim: Incorporation of cutting-edge machine intelligence algorithms is needed to advance the state of the art in image analysis of host–pathogen interaction.
source: To advance the state of the art in image analysis of host–pathogen interaction, incorporation of cutting-edge machine intelligence algorithms (Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014; LeCun et al., 2015) to stratify the image content without the requirement to program complex integrations is needed.
evidence: Statement of need supported by citations to machine learning literature.

claim: HRMAn relies on well-established image segmentation strategies but offers an intuitive integration of deep learning for more complex image analysis.
source: HRMAn relies on the same well-established image segmentation strategies as many other programs but offers an intuitive integration of deep learning for more complex image analysis.
evidence: Description of HRMAn's approach.

claim: Deep neural network-based machine intelligence methods have brought about a revolutionary advance in the field of computer vision.
source: Deep neural network-based machine intelligence methods have brought about a revolutionary advance in the field of computer vision, by allowing for learning of complex morphologies in a highly generalized fashion (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; LeCun et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational deep learning papers.

claim: Deep neural network methods have not been adapted for the field of host–pathogen interaction prior to this work.
source: To date, these methods have not been adapted for the field of host–pathogen interaction.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field at the time of publication.

claim: HCI based fluorescent imaging data from host–pathogen interaction experiments is typically analyzed by classical image segmentation.
source: Typically, HCI based fluorescent imaging data from a host–pathogen interaction experiment is analyzed by classical image segmentation (Osaka et al., 2012; Schmutz et al., 2013; Kühbacher et al., 2015; Ovalle-Bracho et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Segmentation combined with machine learning based on calculated features has occasionally been employed for host-pathogen analysis.
source: Occasionally segmentation combined with machine learning based on calculated features has been employed (Kreibich et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Classical image segmentation and machine learning analysis methods fail at quantifying host protein recruitment to the pathogen.
source: A major short-coming of these classical image segmentation and machine learning analysis methods is that they fail at the level of quantifying host protein recruitment to the pathogen.
evidence: Statement about limitations of existing methods.

claim: Traditional algorithms quantify phenotypes in a rule-based manner, using bulk statistical properties of microscopy images or their segments.
source: This is largely due to the fact that traditional algorithms quantify phenotypes in a rule-based manner, using bulk statistical properties of microscopy images or their segments.
evidence: Explanation of how traditional algorithms work.

claim: Deep neural networks make use of complex patterns within the dataset to learn phenotypes and their diversity.
source: Conversely, deep neural networks make use of complex patterns (e.g. shapes) within the dataset to learn phenotypes and their diversity.
evidence: Explanation of how deep neural networks work.

claim: The neural network derives patterns in an automatic fashion from expert-labelled data.
source: The neural network derives these patterns in an automatic fashion from expert-labelled data.
evidence: Description of neural network training process.

claim: Deep neural networks improve the biological relevance of phenotypic readouts by using pattern complexity to refine classification.
source: Thus, using pattern complexity to refine classification (Krizhevsky et al., 2012), deep neural networks improve the biological relevance of the phenotypic readouts.
evidence: Supported by citation and logical reasoning.

claim: Some proprietary solutions have been employed to extract host protein recruitment data but are impractical and insufficient for most researchers.
source: While some proprietary solutions have been employed to extract host protein recruitment data, these are impractical and insufficient for most researchers as they are tied to single and expensive microscopes and do not operate at human capacity (Polajnar et al., 2017; Touquet et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Artificial intelligence-driven automated analysis for host protein recruitment to pathogens is neither available as open-source nor as a commercial package.
source: To date, for the analysis of host protein recruitment to pathogens, artificial intelligence-driven automated analysis is neither available as an open-source nor as a commercial package.
evidence: Statement about the state of available tools.

claim: There remains a need for an open-source, intuitive, flexible, and trainable host–pathogen interaction analysis software that performs at the level of human analytic capacity.
source: Thus, there remains a need for an open-source, intuitive, flexible, and trainable host–pathogen interaction analysis software that performs at the level of human analytic capacity (Russakovsky et al., 2015; He et al., 2015; Haberl et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of need supported by citations.

claim: HRMAn is a high-throughput, high-content, single-cell image analysis pipeline that incorporates machine learning and a deep convolutional neural network.
source: Here we present a high-throughput, high-content, single-cell image analysis pipeline that incorporates machine learning and a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) ensemble for Host Response to Microbe Analysis (HRMAn; https://hrman.org/).
evidence: Description of the presented tool.

claim: HRMAn is based on the data integration environment KNIME Analytics Platform.
source: To assure its broad applicability to infection biology, HRMAn is based on the data integration environment KNIME Analytics Platform (Berthold et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to KNIME.

claim: The HRMAn analysis relies on training of machine learning algorithms and deep neural networks that can be tailored to individual researchers' needs.
source: The analysis relies on training of machine learning algorithms and deep neural networks that can be tailored to individual researchers' needs.
evidence: Description of HRMAn's flexibility.

claim: HRMAn is designed to work with all file types acquired on any HCI platform or fluorescence microscope.
source: The HRMAn pipeline (Figure 1), is designed to work with all file types acquired on any HCI platform or fluorescence microscope.
evidence: Description of HRMAn's compatibility.

claim: Plate maps including experimental layouts, sample groups and replicates can be loaded into HRMAn.
source: Plate maps including experimental layouts, sample groups and replicates can be loaded, enabling HRMAn to automatically cluster results and perform error analysis.
evidence: Description of HRMAn functionality.

claim: Images are automatically pre-processed and clustered based on user-defined parameters in HRMAn.
source: Once fed into the HRMAn pipeline, images are automatically pre-processed and clustered based on user-defined parameters (i.e. imaging specifications) and corrected for illumination.
evidence: Description of HRMAn processing steps.

claim: In stage 1, HRMAn segments images into pathogen and host cell features for single cell analysis.
source: The subsequent image analysis proceeds in two stages: in stage 1, HRMAn segments images into pathogen and host cell features for single cell analysis.
evidence: Description of HRMAn stage 1 functionality.

claim: HRMAn classifies features using a decision tree learning algorithm previously trained on an annotated dataset.
source: It then classifies these features using a decision tree learning algorithm previously trained on an annotated dataset.
evidence: Description of HRMAn classification method.

claim: In stage 2, HRMAn analyzes host cell features associated with pathogens using a CNN HRMAlexNet trained to distinguish complex phenotypic patterns of host-protein recruitment.
source: In stage 2, HRMAn analyzes host cell features associated with the pathogens using a CNN HRMAlexNet (derived from AlexNet architecture) trained to distinguish complex phenotypic patterns of host-protein recruitment (Krizhevsky et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of HRMAn stage 2 functionality with citation to AlexNet.

claim: Robust classification is achieved by passing segmented regions of interest through multiple non-linear convolutional filters to identify characteristic phenotypic details.
source: Robust classification is achieved by passing segmented regions of interest through multiple non-linear convolutional filters to identify characteristic phenotypic details.
evidence: Description of how HRMAn achieves classification.

claim: HRMAn outputs data as a single spreadsheet file providing ≥15 quantitative descriptions of a pathogen and its interaction with host factors at population and single cell levels.
source: Finally, data are output as a single spreadsheet file providing the researcher with ≥15 quantitative descriptions of a pathogen and its interaction with host factors at population and single cell levels (Figure 1; Readouts).
evidence: Description of HRMAn output with reference to Figure 1.

claim: By separating the analysis, HRMAn offers researchers the flexibility to perform fast, simple quantitative analysis of infection parameters using stage 1, without analyzing host protein recruitment.
source: Importantly, by separating the analysis, HRMAn offers researchers the flexibility to perform fast, simple quantitative analysis of infection parameters using stage 1, without analyzing host protein recruitment.
evidence: Description of HRMAn's modular design.

claim: HRMAn was trained using an annotated dataset of host cells infected with eGFP-expressing Toxoplasma gondii and stained for various host cell features.
source: To train for detection and analysis of host–pathogen interactions, HRMAn was provided an annotated dataset of host cells infected with an eGFP-expressing version of the parasite Toxoplasma gondii (Tg) and stained for various host cell features (Figure 2A) (Seibenhener et al., 2004; Clough et al., 2016).
evidence: Description of training data with citations and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Over 35,000 Tg-vacuoles were analyzed by decision tree, gradient boosted tree, and random forest machine learning classification algorithms and cross-validated.
source: For stage one pathogen detection and enumeration training a simplistic ML strategy – decision tree performed remarkably well. Over 35,000 Tg-vacuoles were analyzed by decision tree, gradient boosted tree, and random forest machine learning classification algorithms and cross-validated (Figure 2B).
evidence: Description of training and validation with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: A simple decision tree with Minimum Description Length pruning was employed for speed and accuracy of pathogen detection (>99.5% for Tg).
source: As each performed equally, a simple decision tree with Minimum Description Length (MDL) pruning, to limit overfitting, was employed for speed and accuracy of pathogen detection (>99.5% for Tg).
evidence: Description of chosen algorithm and its performance.

claim: HRMAn detected and quantified Tg-containing vacuoles harbouring 1, 2, 4 or >4 fluorescent Tg.
source: Using these parameters, in addition to the readouts from stage 1 (see Figure 1), HRMAn detected and quantified Tg-containing vacuoles harbouring 1, 2, 4 or >4 fluorescent Tg (Figure 2C).
evidence: Description of HRMAn capability with reference to Figures 1 and 2C.

claim: The CNN was trained for ubiquitin and p62 recruitment using segmented Tg vacuoles defined in Stage 1.
source: For stage 2, host protein recruitment, the CNN was trained for ubiquitin and p62 recruitment using segmented Tg vacuoles defined in Stage 1.
evidence: Description of stage 2 training.

claim: The deep CNN achieved 92.1% classification accuracy confirmed by expert-based cross-validation after training over 80 epochs.
source: Training over 80 epochs with negative log likelihood as a loss function, the deep CNN achieved 92.1% classification accuracy confirmed by expert-based cross-validation.
evidence: Description of CNN performance.

claim: Precision for 'no recruitment', 'recruitment', and 'artefacts' classes was 0.92, 0.92 and 0.71, while recall was 0.94, 0.89 and 1 respectively.
source: Precision for 'no recruitment', 'recruitment', and 'artefacts' classes was 0.92, 0.92 and 0.71, while recall was 0.94, 0.89 and 1 respectively, hence achieving the accuracy of a human operator and far exceeding human capacity (Figure 2E).
evidence: Quantitative performance metrics with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: The CNN achieved the accuracy of a human operator and far exceeded human capacity.
source: Precision for 'no recruitment', 'recruitment', and 'artefacts' classes was 0.92, 0.92 and 0.71, while recall was 0.94, 0.89 and 1 respectively, hence achieving the accuracy of a human operator and far exceeding human capacity (Figure 2E).
evidence: Claim about performance relative to human capacity with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: More than 98% of all parasites captured in the images have successfully invaded and established a PV, irrespective of the Tg strain used for infection.
source: In a pilot experiment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), staining with the Tg vacuole marker GRA2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) revealed that more than 98% of all parasites captured in the images have successfully invaded and established a PV, irrespective of the Tg strain used for infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Using a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 3 resulted in up to 90% type I and 80% type II Tg infected host cells.
source: Using a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 3 for experiments resulted in up to 90% type I and 80% type II Tg infected host cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: IFNγ treatment did not impact the percentage of infected cells but decreased the number of vacuoles within host cells as well as the number of parasites per cell.
source: Population level readouts from stage one indicated that IFNγ treatment did not impact the percentage of infected cells but decreased the number of vacuoles within host cells as well as the number of parasites per cell (Figure 3A).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: IFNγ treatment resulted in a significant reduction of vacuoles per cell and a minor reduction in mean vacuole size, without impacting vacuole position.
source: At the single cell level, HRMAn found that IFNγ treatment resulted in a significant reduction of vacuoles per cell and a minor reduction in mean vacuole size, without impacting vacuole position (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Both the percentage of replicating parasites and the number of parasites per vacuole were significantly reduced by IFNγ treatment.
source: Concomitant with this reduction in vacuole size, both the percentage of replicating parasites, and the number of parasites per vacuole were significantly reduced by IFNγ treatment (Figure 3C).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: IFNγ−mediated control of Tg in HeLa cells involves both parasite-killing and restriction of Tg replication.
source: Thus, IFNγ−mediated control of Tg in HeLa cells involves both parasite-killing and restriction of Tg replication.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results.

claim: The number of host cells with ubiquitin/p62-positive vacuoles and the percentage of ubiquitin/p62-positive vacuoles per host cell increased with IFNγ.
source: In stage 2, analysis of the >25,000 vacuoles identified in stage 1, showed that the number of host cells with ubiquitin/p62-positive vacuoles and the percentage of ubiquitin/p62-positive vacuoles per host cell increased with IFNγ (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: In untreated cells, only 5.92% of vacuoles were decorated with ubiquitin, p62, or both, which rose to 27.61% in IFNγ-treated cells.
source: Distribution analysis indicated that in untreated cells, only 5.92% of vacuoles were decorated with ubiquitin, p62, or both. This number rose to 27.61% in IFNγ-treated cells, the majority of which (20.92%) were double-positive for ubiquitin/p62 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Quantitative experimental result with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Ubiquitin was more closely associated with Tg vacuoles than p62 and recruitment of both was increased by IFNγ treatment.
source: By quantifying the radial fluorescence intensity distribution of these host factors, HRMAn revealed that ubiquitin was more closely associated with Tg vacuoles than p62 and that recruitment of both was increased by IFNγ treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: p62 binds a ubiquitinated vacuole substrate through its UBA domain.
source: This is in agreement with the notion that p62 binds a ubiquitinated vacuole substrate through its UBA domain (Seibenhener et al., 2004; Clough et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Restriction of Tg replication occurs in vacuoles decorated with ubiquitin/p62.
source: Finally, by analyzing vacuoles that recruit ubiquitin/p62, HRMAn indicated that restriction of Tg replication occurs in vacuoles decorated with these host defense proteins (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: In HeLa cells, IFNγ drives both parasite killing as well as recruitment of ubiquitin/p62 to Tg vacuoles, which acts to restrict parasite replication.
source: Collectively, this data indicates that in HeLa cells, IFNγ drives both parasite killing as well as recruitment of ubiquitin/p62 to Tg vacuoles, which acts to restrict parasite replication (Figure 3).
evidence: Summary conclusion from experimental results with reference to Figure 3.

claim: HRMAn removes experimental size constraints imposed by manual quantification.
source: As a high-throughput, high-content analysis program, HRMAn removes experimental size constraints imposed by manual quantification.
evidence: Statement about HRMAn's capability.

claim: A dose-dependent reduction in Tg infection was seen for each host cell line tested with varying concentrations of IFNγ.
source: First, stage 1 HRMAn was used to ascertain the impact of varying concentrations of IFNγ (50–500 IU/ml) on Tg infection, killing, and replication. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). For each host cell line (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), a dose-dependent reduction in Tg infection was seen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: THP-1s, HFFs, and HUVECs limit infection by IFNγ-dependent Tg killing, while HeLas and A549s do so by restricting replication.
source: Assessment of the vacuole:cell ratio and mean vacuole size indicated that THP-1s, HFFs, and HUVECs limit infection by IFNγ-dependent Tg killing, while HeLas and A549s do so by restricting replication (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: HeLas and A549s acutely restrict type I and type II Tg replication at all concentrations of IFNγ.
source: Quantification of the number of parasites per vacuole indicated that HeLas and A549s acutely restrict type I and type II Tg replication at all concentrations of IFNγ (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C), while THP-1s, HFFs, and HUVECs are far more limited in this capacity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,D–E).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: All host cell types can mediate IFNγ-dependent type I and II Tg killing and growth restriction to similar levels.
source: Taking advantage of the large-scale capabilities of HRMAn, we found that all host cell types can mediate IFNγ-dependent type I and II Tg killing (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C), and growth restriction (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–B) to similar levels.
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Tg vacuoles show strain-dependent (A549, HUVEC), and strain-independent (HFFs) IFNγ-stimulated movement towards the nucleus.
source: Tg vacuoles show strain-dependent (A549, HUVEC), and strain-independent (HFFs) IFNγ-stimulated movement towards the nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Type II Tg grew slower than type I Tg in each host cell line and their growth decreased more upon treatment with IFNγ.
source: HRMAn revealed that type II Tg grew slower than type I Tg in each host cell line and that their growth decreased more upon treatment with IFNγ (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: All cell types could recruit ubiquitin and/or p62 equally well.
source: Consistent with this, stage 2 HRMAn showed that all cell types could recruit ubiquitin and/or p62 equally well (Figure 3—figure supplement 6A), while a greater percentage of type II vacuoles per cell were decorated in response to IFNγ-priming (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: THP-1 cells did not mount a strain-specific response to Tg infection.
source: The exception to this were THP-1 cells, which did not mount a strain-specific response (Figure 3—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: THP-1s display a higher intrinsic capacity to decorate Tg vacuoles than other cell lines, even in the absence of IFNγ.
source: Distribution analysis further indicated that THP-1s display a higher intrinsic capacity to decorate Tg vacuoles than other cell lines, even in the absence of IFNγ (Figure 3—figure supplement 6C).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: No cell-type dependent differences in ubiquitin or p62 coat distance were observed.
source: While no cell-type dependent differences in ubiquitin or p62 coat distance were observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A), THP-1s not only decorate vacuoles with more ubiquitin upon IFNγ stimulation, they also appear to recruit p62 in an IFNγ-independent fashion (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: THP-1s decorate vacuoles with more ubiquitin upon IFNγ stimulation and recruit p62 in an IFNγ-independent fashion.
source: While no cell-type dependent differences in ubiquitin or p62 coat distance were observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A), THP-1s not only decorate vacuoles with more ubiquitin upon IFNγ stimulation, they also appear to recruit p62 in an IFNγ-independent fashion (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Decorated vacuoles in all host cell types displayed a greater ability to restrict the growth of type II versus type I Tg upon IFNγ treatment.
source: Decorated vacuoles in all host cell types displayed a greater ability to restrict the growth of type II versus type I Tg upon IFNγ treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 7C–D).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: HRMAn was trained to recognize Salmonella enterica Typhimurium, a pathogen 16x smaller than Tg.
source: To demonstrate its flexibility, HRMAn was trained to recognize the bacterium Salmonella enterica Typhimurium (STm) - a pathogen 16x smaller than Tg (0.5 μm vs. 8 μm) - and then set to analyze the impact of IFNγ on bacterial killing, replication, and ubiquitin recruitment.
evidence: Description of HRMAn's adaptability with size comparison.

claim: IFNγ treatment in HeLa cells reduced the ratio of STm vacuoles/cell and the bacterial load, without impacting the percent of infected host cells.
source: Stage 1 outputs showed that similar to Tg (Figure 3), IFNγ treatment in HeLa cells reduced the ratio of STm vacuoles/cell and the bacterial load, without impacting the percent of infected host cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figures 3 and 4A.

claim: IFNγ treatment resulted in a significant reduction in the number of STm vacuoles/cell, consistent with a reduction in vacuole size, percent of replicating bacteria, and reduced numbers of STm/vacuole.
source: At the single cell level, HRMAn found a significant reduction in the number of STm vacuoles/cell, consistent with a reduction in vacuole size, percent of replicating bacteria, and reduced numbers of STm/vacuole (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figures 4B-C.

claim: HeLa cells can control infection with STm through IFNγ−dependent bacterial killing and growth restriction.
source: These results demonstrate that HeLa cells can control infection with STm through IFNγ−dependent bacterial killing and growth restriction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results.

claim: The Tg recruitment model was used as input to retrain HRMAn for quantification of ubiquitin recruitment to STm, achieving 69.9% classification accuracy in just 40 epochs using 10-fold less non-augmented image data.
source: For stage 2, we used the Tg recruitment model as input to retrain HRMAn for quantification of ubiquitin recruitment to STm (Figure 4D). This allowed us to achieve 69.9% classification accuracy, confirmed by expert-based cross-validation, in just 40 epochs using 10-fold less non-augmented image data (Figure 4D).
evidence: Description of transfer learning approach and performance with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: HeLa cells restrict STm growth by maintaining vacuole integrity; the small percentage of bacteria that escape vacuoles are decorated with ubiquitin and subsequently cleared by autophagy.
source: It's known that HeLa cells restrict STm growth by maintaining vacuole integrity; the small percentage of bacteria that escape vacuoles are decorated with ubiquitin and subsequently cleared by autophagy (Noad et al., 2017; van Wijk et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The percent of host cells which recruit ubiquitin to STm doubles upon IFNγ treatment, while the percent of decorated vacuoles/cell increases only slightly.
source: Interestingly, stage 2 HRMAn showed that the percent of host cells which recruit ubiquitin to STm doubles upon IFNγ treatment, while the percent of decorated vacuoles/cell increases only slightly (Figure 4E).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: IFNγ does not impact the distance of the ubiquitin coat to STm but increases its thickness.
source: As seen with Tg (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 7A), IFNγ does not impact the distance of the ubiquitin coat to STm but increases its thickness (Figure 4F).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figures 3E, 3—figure supplement 7A, and 4F.

claim: More ubiquitin is recruited to cytosolic STm in the presence of IFNγ and growth of decorated bacteria was restricted.
source: This indicates that more ubiquitin is recruited to cytosolic STm in the presence of IFNγ and growth of decorated bacteria was restricted (Figure 4G).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 4G.

claim: At the single-cell level HeLa cells appear to have reached their capacity for detection and autophagy-mediated clearance of cytosolic/ubiquitinated STm independent of IFNγ treatment.
source: Consequently, although IFNγ treatment increases the number of host cells that recruit ubiquitin to STm and the intensity of that recruitment, at the single-cell level HeLa cells appear to have reached their capacity for detection and autophagy-mediated clearance of cytosolic/ubiquitinated STm independent of IFNγ treatment (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results with reference to Figures 4E-G.

claim: Expression of ROP16 from type I Tg or lack of GRA15 in otherwise isogenic type II parasites reduces the recruitment of murine guanylate binding proteins to the vacuoles.
source: Using transgenic Tg lines expressing different parasite virulence factors, we were able to reproduce and expand upon published data (Virreira Winter et al., 2011). We confirmed that expression of ROP16 from type I Tg or lack of GRA15 in otherwise isogenic type II parasites (PruA7) reduces the recruitment of murine guanylate binding proteins (Gbps) to the vacuoles.
evidence: Experimental result confirming prior work with citation.

claim: Expression of type I ROP18 in type III parasites (CEP) reduced recruitment of murine Gbps 1, 2 and 5 compared to isogenic type III parasites.
source: Similarly, expression of type I ROP18 in type III parasites (CEP) also reduced recruitment of murine Gbps 1, 2 and 5 compared to isogenic type III parasites (Figure 5A).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: HRMAn can be used to study effects of pathogen effector proteins on an established host phenotype.
source: This analysis shows that HRMAn can be used to study effects of pathogen effector proteins on an established host phenotype.
evidence: Conclusion about HRMAn's applicability.

claim: Tg secretes multiple effector proteins upon invasion and during replication, including GRA16, GRA24 and TgIST, that are secreted beyond the boundaries of its PV and subsequently translocated to the host cell nucleus.
source: Tg is known to secret multiple effector proteins upon invasion and during replication. Examples include the parasite proteins GRA16, GRA24 and TgIST, that are secreted beyond the boundaries of its PV and subsequently translocated to the host cell nucleus (Bougdour et al., 2013; Braun et al., 2013; Gay et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HRMAn was able to visualize accumulation of GRA16, GRA24 and TgIST in the nucleus of the host cell.
source: Using HRMAn, we were able to visualize accumulation of these three Tg effector proteins (tagged with an HA-tag) in the nucleus of the host cell.
evidence: Description of HRMAn capability.

claim: The levels of nuclear accumulation of Tg effector proteins correlated to the number of parasites contained within the infected cell.
source: HRMAn, further indicated that the levels of nuclear accumulation correlated to the number of parasites contained within the infected cell (Figure 5B).
evidence: Experimental result with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: HRMAn can be employed to analyze both host and parasite parameters during infection in an unbiased, accurate and high content manner.
source: Thus, HRMAn can be employed to analyze both host and parasite parameters during infection in an unbiased, accurate and high content manner.
evidence: Conclusion about HRMAn's capabilities.

claim: Deep CNNs are a powerful image analysis method inspired by abstraction of animal visual cortex architecture.
source: Recent advances have made deep CNNs a powerful image analysis method (Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014; He et al., 2015; Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015; LeCun et al., 2015; Russakovsky et al., 2015; Haberl et al., 2018). Inspired by abstraction of animal visual cortex architecture, CNNs are able to generalize patterns independent of minor phenotypic differences (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Matsugu et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to deep learning and neuroscience literature.

claim: CNNs are able to generalize patterns independent of minor phenotypic differences.
source: Inspired by abstraction of animal visual cortex architecture, CNNs are able to generalize patterns independent of minor phenotypic differences (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Matsugu et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: HRMAn is a powerful open-source, user-friendly software for the analysis of host–pathogen interaction at the single-cell level combining automated image segmentation, machine learning and a deep CNN.
source: Combining automated image segmentation, machine learning and a deep CNN in an ensemble, HRMAn is a powerful open-source, user-friendly software for the analysis of host–pathogen interaction at the single-cell level.
evidence: Summary statement about HRMAn.

claim: HRMAn is based on the KNIME Analytics Platform which is highly modular, GUI-based and user-friendly.
source: We based HRMAn on the KNIME Analytics Platform (Berthold et al., 2008). Being highly modular, GUI-based and user-friendly, HRMAn can rapidly be updated with latest technological advances, yet remains transparent for the average user.
evidence: Description of platform choice with citation.

claim: The ready-to-use DL4J library modules employed in HRMAn allow for incorporation of the latest advances in artificial intelligence in a click-through manner with zero coding.
source: Furthermore, the ready-to-use DL4J library modules we employed allow for incorporation of the latest advances in the field of artificial intelligence in a click-through manner with zero coding.
evidence: Description of HRMAn's implementation.

claim: HRMAn represents the only open-source CNN-driven host-pathogen analysis solution for fluorescent images to date.
source: To date, HRMAn represents the only open-source CNN-driven host-pathogen analysis solution for fluorescent images.
evidence: Statement about HRMAn's uniqueness in the field.

claim: More complex CNN architectures can be easily implemented through recently introduced KNIME-Keras integration, which may facilitate improvement in classification accuracy.
source: While HRMAlexNet is a rather simple architecture, more complex architectures can be easily implemented through recently introduced KNIME-Keras integration (Chollet, 2015), which may facilitate improvement in the classification accuracy.
evidence: Statement about future improvements with citation.

claim: HRMAn moves the phenotype of host defense protein recognition of pathogens into the realm of HCI at the level of artificial intelligence and human accuracy and capacity.
source: This is important, as it moves the phenotype of host defense protein recognition of pathogens into the realm of HCI at the level of artificial intelligence and thus human accuracy and capacity.
evidence: Statement about HRMAn's significance.

claim: When presented with the problem of classifying host protein recruitment to a pathogen, inaccurate classical image segmentation could lead to erroneous results.
source: However, when presented with the problem of classifying host protein recruitment to a pathogen, inaccurate classical image segmentation could lead to erroneous results.
evidence: Statement about limitations of classical methods.

claim: Employing an artificial intelligence algorithm, HRMAn circumvents problems of classical segmentation and delivers user-defined automated and unbiased enumeration of host-pathogen interplay.
source: Employing an artificial intelligence algorithm, HRMAn circumvents these problems and delivers user-defined automated and unbiased enumeration of this subset of the host-pathogen interplay.
evidence: Statement about HRMAn's advantages.

claim: HRMAn is capable of detecting and quantifying multiple pathogen and host parameters using Tg and STm infection models.
source: Using Tg and STm infection models, we demonstrate that HRMAn is capable of detecting and quantifying multiple pathogen and host parameters.
evidence: Summary of demonstrated capabilities.

claim: HRMAn can be adapted easily to two entirely different pathogens that differ in size by a magnitude and display distinct growth rates and infection dynamics.
source: Importantly, we show that HRMAn can be adapted easily to two entirely different pathogens, that not only differ in size by a magnitude, but also display distinct growth rates and infection dynamics.
evidence: Statement about HRMAn's adaptability demonstrated in the study.

claim: HRMAn requires no coding or specialized computer science knowledge and is designed for biologists.
source: Designed for biologists, HRMAn requires no coding or specialized computer science knowledge.
evidence: Description of HRMAn's user-friendliness.

claim: HRMAn's modular architecture and use of KNIME allows users to tailor experimental outputs to their own datasets and questions.
source: Its modular architecture and the use of KNIME, which provides a graphical representation of the analysis pipeline, allows users to tailor experimental outputs to their own datasets and questions.
evidence: Description of HRMAn's flexibility.

claim: The models generated by HRMAn can be used as primers to lower the training dataset size, computation power and training time requirements.
source: As the models we have generated can be used as primers to lower the training dataset size, computation power and training time requirements, HRMAn can be rapidly applied to similar large-scale, image-based experimental setups.
evidence: Statement about transfer learning capability.

claim: HRMAn will allow a broad range of researchers to extend into the realm of high-throughput, unbiased, quantitative single-cell analysis of host–pathogen interaction.
source: As such, HRMAn will allow a broad range of researchers to extend into the realm of high-throughput, unbiased, quantitative single-cell analysis of host–pathogen interaction.
evidence: Statement about HRMAn's potential impact.

claim: All open-source KNIME workflows used in this publication are available at https://github.com/HRMAn-Org/HRMAn and https://hrman.org/ under GPLv3 open-source software license.
source: All open-source KNIME workflows used in this publication can be found at: https://github.com/HRMAn-Org/HRMAn and on the homepage https://hrman.org/ under GPLv3 open-source software license to allow for rapid and open dissemination and free availability for the research community.
evidence: Statement about code availability.

claim: HRMAlexNet architecture consisted of a total of 5 convolutional layers.
source: Our architecture consisted of a total of 5 convolutional layers, where the first two were immediately followed by local response normalization layers and max pooling layers.
evidence: Description of neural network architecture.

claim: HRMAlexNet was based on the open source DeepLearning4J library implementation in KNIME Analytics Platform.
source: To ensure our neural network can be implemented by other researchers with no coding, it was based on the open source DeepLearning4J library implementation in KNIME Analytics Platform.
evidence: Description of implementation choice.

claim: HRMAlexNet has two fully connected layers instead of three, which pushes the fitting burden more to the convolutional layers.
source: HRMAlexNet has two fully connected layers instead of three, which pushes the fitting burden more to the convolutional layers (Figure 1).
evidence: Description of architectural difference with reference to Figure 1.

claim: HRMAlexNet was designed to take 100 by 100 by two pixels images as input.
source: We have changed the input layer dimensions to fit the multichannel fluorescence microscopy data, since our input two channels, rather than the standard RGB dimension of three. Hence, unlike the original AlexNet, HRMAlexNet was suited to take 100 by 100 by two pixels images as input and designed to run on a single graphic processing unit (GPU).
evidence: Description of input specifications.

claim: The ADAM learning rate update algorithm was substituted for Stochastic Gradient Descent with Nesterov momentum because SGD was failing to converge on fluorescence microscopy data.
source: While optimizing the network's hyperparameters, we found that learning rate updating algorithm proposed by default in the KNIME architecture, as well as in Krizhevsky et al. - Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with Nesterov momentum - was failing to converge on our fluorescence microscopy data (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Therefore, we have substituted this algorithm for the more advanced learning rate update algorithm ADAM (Kingma and Ba, 2014) with both mean and Variance decay parameters, which proved to converge well on various data and initial learning rate ranges.
evidence: Description of optimization process with citations.

claim: The choice of DeepLearning4J as a deep learning library allowed use of 16-bit microscopy images directly, preventing information loss upon conversion of scientific imaging data.
source: The choice of DeepLearning4J as a deep learning library allowed us to use 16-bit microscopy images directly, preventing information loss upon conversion of scientific imaging data.
evidence: Statement about technical advantage of library choice.

claim: Neural networks were trained using SGD based backpropagation with ADAM updater over at least 80 epochs.
source: Our neural networks were trained using SGD based backpropagation (using ADAM updater with ADAM Mean Decay of 0.9 and ADAM Variance Decay of 0.999 (Kingma and Ba, 2014)) on the augmented original data over at least 80 epochs.
evidence: Description of training procedure with citation.

claim: Training was performed in mini-batches of 200 to fully utilize GPU capacity.
source: To fully utilize the GPU capacity, training was performed in mini-batches of 200.
evidence: Description of training parameter.

claim: Xavier algorithm was employed for weight initialization strategy and negative log likelihood as loss function.
source: We employed the Xavier algorithm for the weight initialization strategy and negative log likelihood (NLL) as our loss function (Kingma and Ba, 2014).
evidence: Description of training parameters with citation.

claim: Data augmentation was performed using various rotations, image reflecting, and image translation within the field of view.
source: During the augmentation processing, the original labelled dataset was concatenated with a modified version of it. The modifications included various rotations, image reflecting, image translation within the field of view.
evidence: Description of data augmentation methods.

claim: Microscopy data are typically rotation-, translation- or reflection-invariant.
source: As microscopy data are typically rotation-, translation- or reflection-invariant, such modification allowed us to create a better dataset aiming at a more generalized model.
evidence: Statement about properties of microscopy data justifying augmentation approach.

claim: Model validation was performed using the non-augmented test fraction of the labelled dataset previously unseen by the model.
source: Model validation was performed using the non-augmented test fraction of the labelled dataset previously unseen by the model.
evidence: Description of validation procedure.

claim: HRMAn automatically detected and analyzed more than 15,000 HeLa cells resulting in 15 quantitative outputs of host–pathogen interaction.
source: HRMAn automatically detected and analyzed more than 15,000 HeLa cells resulting in 15 quantitative outputs of host–pathogen interaction (Figure 3).
evidence: Quantitative description of analysis scale with reference to Figure 3.

claim: A reduction in the ratio between vacuoles and host cells serves as an indirect measurement for parasite killing.
source: As eGFP fluorescence is lost when parasites are killed, a reduction in the ratio between vacuoles and host cells serves as an indirect measurement for parasite killing.
evidence: Explanation of measurement interpretation.

claim: HeLa cells restrict the growth of Tg through ubiquitination of parasitophorous vacuoles and subsequent non-canonical, p62-dependent autophagy.
source: Previous reports indicate that HeLa cells restrict the growth of Tg through ubiquitination of parasitophorous vacuoles and subsequent non-canonical, p62-dependent autophagy (Selleck et al., 2015; Clough et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.
